segments.text: So, we continue introduction to French with a new student. Welcome Ed. The word for what in French is
q, q-u-e, pronounced q, q. What was to eat? Manger. And you eat? Tu mange. Good. We have an
e s ending, but we don't hear that. It's just like manger, but without the e ending. Tu
mange. Are you eating? Tu mange. Or? Mange-tu. Very good. Mange-tu. We could make the
inversion there. We have the option. It's slightly more informal, slightly more
familiar to say. Tu mange. Mange-tu. What are you eating? Que mange-tu? Very good. Que
mange-tu? So when we have a question word at the beginning, like que, the inversion that
we make for the question, it's no longer optional. We need to do it. Que mange-tu. We
couldn't say que tu manges. I know in French is je sais, je sais, I know, je sais. This
is spelled s-a-i-s. And it's related to sapien in homo sapien. That's the knowing
being, the wise being, the homo sapien. So I know, je sais. Je sais. I don't know. Je
ne sais pas. Je ne sais pas. Very good. I know nothing. Je ne sais rien. Very good. Je
ne sais rien. And then what was the word for what? Que. Que also means that in the sense
of I know that you want to eat. So I think that it's okay. So how would you say that?
I know that you want to eat. I know that you want to eat. Je sais que tu veux manger. Very good. Je
sais que tu veux manger. To come in French is venir. To come. So again the E is like
venir. Much better. And it ends I are like finir, for example, to finish. And this
vun of venir is a very busy building block. We have it all over. It's what we have
in souvenir, in avenue, revenue, convenient. Convenient is when things come together. Adventure
that you have the vun of venir. Again convention, convent, intervene. So we have
venir to come. Venir. Very good. I know that you want to come. I know that you want to come.
Je sais que tu veux venir. So que is that in this sense of the word now? I know that you want to come.
And also the word for what? You know is tu sais. Tu sais, you know. Do you know?
C'est tout. C'est tu. Tu sais. Do you know it? Tu le sais. Good. Tu le sais or le sais tu. So this is
what you would say as a complete sentence in French. If you were to say do you know as a
complete sentence you would say do you know it? Tu le sais. What do you know?
Que tu sais? Que c'est tout? Very good. Que c'est tout. Very good. So because we have the question
word there, que, we need to make that inversion. Que c'est tout. But we've also seen how we can
put the question word after the verb in French and avoid the inversion. We can say you know what
rather than what do you know. But if we want to put what after to avoid that inversion,
you know what and be a bit more informal or a bit more familiar. The word for what is no longer
que but quoi. We use a different word for what. Quoi. Quoi. So if you want to say you know what,
tu sais quoi. Tu sais quoi. This may be because as we saw que also means that and tu sais que. Maybe
misunderstood like you know that and we'd be waiting to hear what. So we use quoi when
what comes after the verb. Tu sais quoi. And tu sais quoi is used a lot like you know what you know
when you have something surprising to say. It's used a lot like that in French. Tu sais
quoi you know what. This quoi is also what we have in the English French expression when we
say it has a certain je ne sais quoi. It has a certain I don't know what which is used in
French too. Tell me again what was to eat. Manger. Manger. I eat. Je mange. So we have in sound
manger without the ending. Mange. But in writing M-A-N-G-E to make sure that we hear that final
no. Je mange. He eats. Il mange. Spell the same as je mange. You eat. Tu mange. Tu mange. This has
an S on the end but of course we don't hear it. Tu mange. What are you eating? Tu mange quoi.
Tu mange quoi. Or if you wanted to use que, how would it be? Que mange tu? Que mange tu. Very good.
Quoi. Quoi is also what you would use in exclamation rather than que. You would say
quoi? What? So this form isn't only for when we have what on the end of the question. In fact
the word for why in French is built with quoi. Pour quoi. Literally for what?
Pour quoi. For what? Why? And that's one word. Pourquoi. Pourquoi. Why don't you want to eat?
Why don't you want to eat? Pourquoi tu ne veux pas manger. Very good. Pourquoi tu ne veux pas manger.
And with pourquoi we don't have to make an inversion anymore. You felt that because you said
pourquoi tu ne veux. And this is probably because French decides that the question can be
contained in that question phrase. Even though that's one word. Pourquoi. It literally means
because of what for what. And there the question is kind of contained in there. So even though we
have that at the beginning we don't need to make the inversion if we don't want to. Pourquoi tu
ne veux pas manger. Or of course with the inversion. Pourquoi ne veux tu pas manger. Why don't you
want to eat anything. Pourquoi tu ne veux pas manger rien. Non. Pourquoi tu ne veux rien manger. Good. So rien
replaces pas. So our negation. Now normal everyday negation is ne pas. But then we can have
variations on that. No. So ne pas gives us don't or not. But then ne rien gives us not anything.
Pourquoi tu ne veux rien manger. Very good.
